title: Hamming vs Bluejay in 2026: Human Review and Pricing Compared
summary: Hamming vs Bluejay compared on who they're built for, human review, integrations, release workflow, and pricing, as of October 2026. See the comparison.
body_markdown:
If Hamming and Bluejay are both on your shortlist, you’ve probably noticed how alike they look. Both run simulated callers against your voice agent, score its production calls with an AI judge (an LLM that grades each conversation), and are SOC 2 Type II and HIPAA compliant. So where do they actually differ, and does that difference matter for your team?


Hamming vs Bluejay comes down to two things: the extent of human review and whether you can see the price before a sales call. Hamming sends flagged calls to reviewers, who grade them on scorecards, and neither of its plans lists a price: both say “Request a demo.” Bluejay’s review centers on compliance, flagging non-compliant calls for someone to check, and it publishes its prices, starting at $0 a month plus usage. For a team in finance, healthcare, or insurance, though, neither difference settles the question that matters most: can you show your compliance team that the judge’s scores hold up?


Here’s how the two compare, drawn from each vendor’s public pages and our own review of the field, as of October 2026.


Criterion Hamming Bluejay


Company and focus Seed-stage; audio-first evaluation and monitoring for voice agents Seed-stage, founded 2025; auto-generated simulations for voice and chat agents


Human review Flagged calls go to reviewers with scorecards Flags non-compliant calls for review


LiveKit WebRTC with your API key, secret, and server URL; captures transcripts, audio, and tool calls Direct, SIP, and outbound test paths; scores live calls by webhook or API

Pricing and access Production and Enterprise plans, both “Request a demo,” with no prices; no traditional self-serve free trial $0 a month plus usage, $500, $1,000; Enterprise custom


## Hamming and Bluejay are seed-stage tools with different focuses


Both companies are early. Hamming announced a $3.8 million seed round in December 2024, and it focuses on evaluating and monitoring voice agents from the call audio. Bluejay was[founded in 2025](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/bluejay) and has raised a $4 million seed round. Its focus is auto-generated simulation: it creates test calls for voice and chat agents automatically.


Whatever the focus, a regulated business hits the same moment: someone asks why a test failed a release or why a production call was flagged, and the platform has to show its judge got it right. Human review is how a platform shows that, and it’s where Hamming and Bluejay differ most.


## Human review is where Hamming and Bluejay differ most


An AI judge is only worth trusting if it agrees with the people who would otherwise listen to the calls. Human review is how you find out: people check the calls the judge scored.


Hamming’s pitch highlights how accurate its judge is, and flagged calls go to reviewers, who grade them on scorecards. Bluejay’s review centers on compliance: it flags non-compliant calls for someone to check.


Sending a call to a person is one step. Knowing how often the judge misses a failure your reviewers would catch is another, and it’s the question a compliance team will ask. We come back to it in the last section.


## If your agent runs on LiveKit: how each one connects


Both are listed as testing partners in[LiveKit’s testing docs](https://docs.livekit.io/testing/) , so either can reach a LiveKit agent. They differ in how a test caller gets into the room, what you configure, and how your live calls get scored.


Hamming tests LiveKit agents over[WebRTC](https://hamming.ai/integrations/livekit) . You add your LiveKit API key, secret, and server URL, then choose whether Hamming provisions the rooms or uses rooms you control. Each test run captures transcripts, audio recordings, and tool call data.


Bluejay[documents three test paths](https://docs.getbluejay.ai/integrations/livekit.md) . Direct connects to your agent without phone audio, for iterating on agent logic. SIP tests the same route your phone calls take. Outbound is for agents that place calls: your agent dials Bluejay’s simulated callers. To score live calls, you send them to Bluejay through the LiveKit webhook or from your agent through its API.


## Release workflow: running the same tests on every change


Tests pay off when they run on every change, not only when someone remembers to start them. Hamming runs from its browser app, an API, and GitHub Actions, and its[documentation](https://docs.hamming.ai/) needs an access code. Bluejay runs from an API and GitHub Actions, with public docs.


## Hamming vs Bluejay pricing: published plans versus a sales call


Bluejay[publishes its plans](https://getbluejay.ai/pricing) : $0 a month plus usage, Growth at $500 a month, Scale at $1,000 a month, and a custom Enterprise plan. Hamming lists no prices:[both of its plans](https://hamming.ai/pricing) , Production and Enterprise, say “Request a demo,” and its quote depends on the agents you run and the calls they take. Its[FAQ](https://hamming.ai/faqs) says, “We don’t offer a traditional free trial with self-serve access.”


## Where Coval fits for regulated teams


Hamming and Bluejay give you the same testing baseline and differ on what their human review covers and whether you see a price up front. If you have to defend a score to a compliance team, neither difference answers your real question: does the judge catch the failures your own reviewers find? Coval is built to answer it, and it plugs into the agent stack and release pipeline you already run.


Coval puts your reviewers at the center. Rules you set add calls to a[review queue](https://www.coval.ai/products/human-review/) automatically, and failures, edge cases, and low-confidence calls go to the top, so nobody wades through a random sample. Every override and annotation your reviewers make is tracked, which gives your compliance team its audit trail. If you don’t have an in-house QA team, Coval offers[labeling as a service](https://www.coval.ai/blog/how-to-create-ai-judge-metrics-you-can-trust/) : trained reviewers who label your calls and calibrate your metrics for you.


Then we measure the judge against your reviewers’ answers, because a high agreement number can hide a judge that misses every failure. Our[docs](https://docs.coval.ai/concepts/metrics/human-review/insights) give an example: if reviewers pass 95 of 100 conversations, a metric that passes all 100 agrees with them 95% of the time and catches none of the five failures. That’s why we also measure catch rate, the share of the failures your reviewers found that the judge flagged too. The metric that passed all 100 has a catch rate of zero.


We build for regulated enterprises in[financial services](https://www.coval.ai/industries/financial-services/) ,[healthcare](https://www.coval.ai/industries/healthcare/) , and[insurance](https://www.coval.ai/industries/insurance/) . Hamming serves a broad mix of industries and, in our view, is less focused on those teams. We raised a[$28 million Series A](https://www.coval.ai/blog/coval-series-a/) in June 2026, bringing our total to $31 million, and our founder, Brooke Hopkins,[led evaluation job infrastructure](https://www.coval.ai/about-us/) at Waymo before starting the company. Chime tests its voice agents with Coval, and Perplexity and Fortune 500 enterprises are among the[more than 60 organizations](https://www.coval.ai/blog/new-self-improving-agents/) that use it.


Coval covers the same baseline as Hamming and Bluejay, and it’s SOC 2 Type II and HIPAA compliant too. Our simulated callers sound like real callers, with the accents and background noise you choose. Coval’s[LiveKit connection](https://docs.coval.ai/concepts/agents/connections/livekit) works with LiveKit Cloud and self-hosted deployments, and it needs two settings: your LiveKit server URL and a token endpoint. That’s a small endpoint you run that hands Coval a LiveKit access token, so the credentials that sign it stay on your side. In CI, the[GitHub Action](https://github.com/coval-ai/coval-github-action) launches a Coval run and fails the job if any simulation returns the metric value you’ve marked as a failure. And you can see the price before a sales call: as of October 2026, Coval’s[plans](https://www.coval.ai/pricing/) cost $100 a month for Starter, $500 for Growth, and from $4,500 for Enterprise.
